title: Greenpeace drops boulders in North Sea fishing grounds off Norfolk
summary:
Greenpeace has dropped nine boulders off the east coast of England to create a barrier that disrupts bottom trawling by fishing vessels.
The environmental campaigners' ship Arctic Sunrise released the rocks, without a licence, over the weekend about 50km (30 miles) east of Great Yarmouth, Norfolk.
Greenpeace claimed it had "effectively closed 116 sq km (45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA) to bottom trawling".
When asked if it had permission to drop the boulders, Greenpeace said this was a "last resort" for it, and it did not have a licence.
It said that after years of meeting with politicians and the government to try to protect marine protected areas, progress had been "at a glacial pace".

title: Exclusive: Most voters believe climate change threatens the American Dream
summary:
This story is part of the series The Dream That Oil Built , which explores the connections between climate change, fossil fuels, and the American Dream.
Voters, on the other hand, view climate change itself as a problem for their aspirations.
“We identify a strong concern about climate change as a threat to achieving the American Dream,” said Grace Adcox, a senior climate strategist at the progressive think tank.
Cost of living tops voters’ worries about the American Dream; climate change ranks last Share of likely voters who named each as the greatest threat today to their ability to achieve or maintain the American Dream 5 percent said they didn’t know.
Why do so many people think climate change will hurt the American Dream, if it’s so close to the bottom of the list of their concerns today?

title: Broughshane Waterfowl Park: Recovery effort continues after oil tank vandalism
summary:
Recovery efforts are continuing after an oil spill caused by the vandalism of a nearby home heating oil tank resulted in the death of 13 birds from Broughshane Waterfowl Park.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters last week for urgent specialist care, but the death toll has continued to rise.
The popular attraction in County Antrim has been forced to close while efforts continue to remove oil from the pond.
Police have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.

title: Not Wind, Not Solar: Japan's Renewable Project Makes Energy From Saltwater
summary:
Wind and solar power are both well established sources of renewable energy, but for nations with plenty of coastline, a promising emerging technology called osmotic power offers another possibility.
Osmotic power involves generating electricity from the natural interaction between saltwater and freshwater, and Japan has turned the intriguing idea into a working power plant.
The technology uses a membrane that separates saltwater from freshwater.
The membrane allows water molecules to pass through from the freshwater side into the saltwater side, while blocking most of the salt.
Japan, a country that's no stranger to exploring new energy technologies, began operating the osmotic power facility in the western city of Fukuoka in 2025 using concentrated brine left over from seawater desalination alongside treated wastewater.

title: No need for more PM2.5 forecasts as too many indicators may confuse public: Grace Fu
summary:
SINGAPORE: Singapore does not need additional PM2.5 forecasts as too many indicators may confuse the public, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said on Tuesday (Nov 3).
Ms Fu said the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) and hourly readings of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) have worked well in guiding decisions.
“We don’t think there is a need to include 12-hour, 24-hour or 48-hour PM2.5 forecasts as having too many indicators may complicate our public messages,” she said.
Ms Fu said the daily PSI forecast helps the public plan activities for the next day, while hourly PM2.5 readings can guide immediate outdoor activities.
In response to Mr Fadli's supplementary questions on whether the government can provide PM2.5 forecasts or qualitative trend indicators, Ms Fu said the current system is the right one.
